classification.difficultyReason: Students convert both speeds into vertical rises, choose a distance at the shared endpoint or an equivalent starting point, and construct a distance–time graph that satisfies both secant constraints.

content.prompt: The graph of a car’s distance–time relationship is missing, but you know that between 1 and 3 seconds, the average speed is $10\text{ m/s}$, and between 3 and 5 seconds, it is $14\text{ m/s}$. Construct a plausible distance–time graph.

answer.short: One possible graph is $d=t^2+6t$ for $0\le t\le5$, with $d$ in metres and $t$ in seconds.
answer.worked:
One possible distance model is $d(t)=t^2+6t$, giving $d(1)=7$, $d(3)=27$ and $d(5)=55$ metres.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Average speed on }[1,3]&=\frac{27-7}{3-1}\\\text{Average speed on }[1,3]&=10\text{ m/s}\\\text{Average speed on }[3,5]&=\frac{55-27}{5-3}\\\text{Average speed on }[3,5]&=14\text{ m/s}\end{align*}$$

The increasing curve shown satisfies both conditions. Other graphs with the same changes in distance over these intervals are possible.

spec.description: Authored example graph, not a supplied student scaffold. An increasing parabola passes through (1,7), (3,27) and (5,55); dashed guides identify those coordinates.
spec.mathematics: d(t)=t^2+6t for 0<=t<=5; secant gradients are 10 and 14 m/s on the requested intervals.
